program: Inglês Geral & Intercultural -- Fluência e Autonomia
hub_subtitle: Inglês para a vida real — falar, entender qualquer sotaque e ter autonomia no idioma

lesson.menu_desc: A suitcase from a Hamburg flea market, a desk with a letter from 1916 and a clock that everybody stops to look at. Tonight, who, which, that, whose and where -- and the commas that change the meaning
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 18 -- The Story Behind the Object
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Claudia Veraldi | Lesson 18 -- The Story Behind the Object

listenings.text: My name is Greta, and I live in Hamburg. Every Sunday I go to the flea market, which is next to the river. Three years ago I saw an old brown suitcase, which was covered with hotel labels from the nineteen fifties: Rome, Lisbon, Cairo. The man who was selling it wanted forty euros. We haggled for ten minutes, which is completely normal at a German flea market, and I paid twenty-five. At home I opened it and found a name inside the lid: Hannelore Weiss. I was curious, so I searched online, and I found a woman whose grandmother had that name. She lived in a small town near Bremen. I wrote to her, and she cried on the phone. The suitcase was the one that her grandmother took on her honeymoon. I gave it back to her. I did not ask for the twenty-five euros. Some things have a value that you cannot put on a price tag.

I am Tom, and I restore old furniture in a small workshop in York, which used to be a bakery. People think my job is about wood and glue, but really it is about stories. A few years ago, a lady brought me a writing desk that she had bought at an auction. One of the drawers, which had been stuck for decades, would not open. When I finally got it open, I found a letter. It was from a young soldier who was writing to his mother in nineteen sixteen. He told her not to worry, and he asked her to save him some of her apple cake. We never found out if he came home. The lady, whose own grandfather had been a soldier, decided not to sell the desk. She framed the letter and put it on the wall, right above the desk. That desk was worth about two hundred pounds. Now it is worth its weight in gold.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: The skill of making things carefully by hand
A valuable object that a family keeps for generations
Importance that comes from memories, not from money
The soft shine an old surface gets with time and use
An outdoor market that sells old and used things
Old, but of good quality and still valued today
Owned by someone else before you
To give something to a younger person in your family

vocab.text: Three of tonight’s words are whole expressions: a diamond in the rough, worth its weight in gold and one man’s trash is another man’s treasure. And notice an heirloom: the h is silent, so it sounds like an AIR-loom.

items.situation: Point to one object near you and say who gave it to you. Use who or that.
tips: This is the lamp that my sister gave me.
Defining: it tells you WHICH lamp. No commas.

items.situation: Add an extra detail about your town, with commas.
tips: My town, which has about forty thousand people, is very quiet.

items.situation: Describe a person by something that belongs to them. Use whose.
tips: She is the neighbor whose garden is full of roses.

items.situation: Tell me about a place where you love to buy old or used things.
tips: There is a small antiques shop where I always find something interesting.
Where for places. Do not add there at the end.

items.situation: You are at a flea market and the price is too high. Haggle politely.
tips: It is lovely, but it is a bit more than I wanted to spend. Would you take thirty?
Callback from lesson 14: polite and tactful.

items.situation: Tell me about something that has sentimental value for you.
tips: My father’s old watch, which does not work anymore, has a lot of sentimental value.
This one has no grammar target. Say the true thing.

answerkey.title: Reveal the answer key
key: who for people: the man who sold me the chair.
which for things: the desk, which was stuck for decades.
that for people or things, but ONLY without commas: the clock that my grandfather bought.
whose for possession: the woman whose table I restored.
where for places: the market where I found it (no there at the end).
No commas = defining: it tells you WHICH one.
Commas = non-defining: one more detail. Never that. In speech, a small pause before and after.
And the one that is not grammar: haggling is normal at a flea market in Hamburg or London, but in a shop it can be a faux pas.

paras: A new object has a price. An old object has a biography. The chair that you buy in a shop today knows nothing. The chair which you find at a flea market has already lived a whole life: the family who bought it, the kitchen where it stood, the children whose shoes scratched its legs.

This is why restorers often say that the best part of their work is not the wood or the paint. It is the surprises. A restorer in York once opened a writing desk, which had been closed for decades, and found a letter that a soldier wrote to his mother in 1916. The desk, which was worth about two hundred pounds, suddenly had a value that no price tag could show.

Different cultures treat old things in different ways. In Germany, almost every city has a Sunday flea market, where people haggle happily over a lamp or a suitcase. In many Brazilian families, old furniture was simply replaced by something new, and the past went to the street. Today that is changing, and second-hand is becoming a choice, not a necessity.
So next time you see an old object, ask the question that collectors always ask: not how much is it? but who had it before me?

reading.prompt: Read once, quickly. Which title fits the whole text best?
choices: How to find cheap furniture at flea markets in Germany and Brazil
Old objects carry the stories of the people who owned them
Why restorers prefer wood to paint

items: The text says a new chair from a shop already has a story.
It says the new chair knows nothing; the old one has already lived a whole life.
According to restorers, the best part of the work is the surprises.
Not the wood or the paint: the surprises.
The letter in the desk was written by a mother to her son.
A soldier wrote it to his mother, in 1916.
In German flea markets, people often haggle.
People haggle happily over a lamp or a suitcase.
In the sentence The desk, which was worth about two hundred pounds, the part between the commas tells you which desk.
It only adds extra information. We already know which desk.

lesson.grammar_point: defining and non-defining relative clauses with who, which, that, whose and where
